prize_parts.citation: For the development of general palladium-catalyzed carbon-nitrogen cross-coupling

statement.case_for: Buchwald-Hartwig amination is the one candidacy where the opening ballots converge on both the achievement and the names: five members ranked it and all five proposed the same two laureates. The attribution is as clean as this list offers. Ligand design (bulky biaryl phosphines and chelating bisphosphines) was grounded in an understanding of oxidative addition, amine binding and reductive elimination, so the mechanism is part of the achievement and not an afterthought. Three decades of independent confirmation and industrial use mean that no one can call it early. The 2010 prize recognised C-C coupling (Heck, Negishi, Suzuki), not C-N bond formation, so the chemistry is distinct. My own first-place candidate, long-range electron transfer through proteins (B043, Gray and Winkler), is scientifically the one I care most about, but it has no support beyond my own ballot. A committee member who takes the procedure seriously should say so and not push a configuration the expert reports have not yet put on the table.
statement.case_against: The 2010 cross-coupling prize may leave some colleagues feeling that Pd coupling has been honoured. Kosugi's tin-amide coupling (and Migita-type precedent) leaves a real priority question: if it is more than a footnote, the three-name limit is strained, and a stoichiometric-tin method does not obviously support a laureate. The case also rests on a method rather than a single conceptual discovery. My own field is not synthetic chemistry, so I would want the expert report on organometallic catalysis to confirm that Buchwald and Hartwig are the decisive pair and that later ligand developers are not owed equal credit. I rank it ahead of B043 and B058 here because I expect it to survive scrutiny, not because I find it the deepest science.

responses.point: Somfai ranks C-N coupling first. He sees ligand-enabled general amination as a routine, broadly used tool in medicinal and process chemistry, and treats Kosugi's tin-amide work as a precursor whose status is a judgment call.
responses.response: I agree on the pair and on the distinction from the 2010 prize, and your point that C-N coupling was not what that prize cited is the strongest answer to the overlap worry. I would not dismiss Kosugi as a footnote without evidence. The report should state precisely what the tin-amide chemistry showed (scope, catalytic versus stoichiometric, mechanism). If it showed catalytic amination in a general sense, the priority question is serious. Your organic-chemistry judgment is needed here, since I cannot settle it from my own field.

responses.point: Linke, the chair, ranks phase separation (B046) first. He sees a physically clean thermodynamic framework with very broad impact, and he acknowledges that the interpretation of in-cell condensates is still debated.
responses.response: I share your taste for mechanism stated in physical terms, and the P-granule and multivalent-protein work is exactly that. My reservation is the one you raised yourself: which cellular structures are equilibrium phase-separated and functionally relevant is not stable. I would prefer to see that settled before the committee commits, especially with five credited names and an unresolved third slot among Rosen, Pappu and Mittag. I also note that your own ballot gives C-N coupling a two-name configuration, so I think you may not oppose B035 as strongly as your rank of 8 suggests.

responses.point: Aqvist ranks massively parallel sequencing (B011) first. He argues that its chemistry and consequences make it the clearest game-changer and that recognition is overdue.
responses.response: I accept that its impact is enormous and that Solexa chemistry is real chemistry. My difficulty is attribution, which you also flag: reversible-terminator sequencing and the 454 pyrosequencing platform are different technology lineages, Ju and Mayer have claims, and Linke would credit only two people while you and others would credit three. That is a harder allocation problem than Buchwald and Hartwig, and I would want the expert report on the sequencing field to say which lineage is the chemical core before I could support a specific trio.

responses.point: Zou ranks the nitrogenase structures and mechanism (B058) second and the molecular-sieve design candidacy (B002) first. On nitrogenase she notes that the structures are well confirmed but the catalytic mechanism is unresolved, so recognition would rest on the structural work.
responses.response: We agree on B058, which I also ranked second, and on its limits. The first MoFe-protein and FeMo-cofactor structures (Rees) and the interstitial carbide (Einsle) are secure. The N2 binding mode and the sequence of electron and proton delivery are not, so a citation could honestly cover only the structure of the cofactor, and Seefeldt's mechanistic role would then be harder to justify. That weakens its readiness against C-N coupling this year, but I think it should remain a strong alternative.

responses.point: Chabes ranks targeted protein degradation (B010) first. He argues that PROTACs and molecular glues turn ubiquitin-proteasome biology into a designable chemical principle, and that the cereblon mechanism makes the glue pharmacology explicable.
responses.response: The cereblon mechanism for thalidomide-class drugs is a real mechanistic result, and I do not dispute the principle. My concern is the same one you list: the PROTAC strand (Crews, Deshaies) and the glue-mechanism strand (Handa, Ito) are different discoveries, while Ciulli and Gray are not covered by the Aili/Aqvist/Chabes trio. The committee would be choosing among at least five or six deserving people, and no PROTAC drug is yet approved. I would not call it premature, but I would want the report to say whether this is one achievement or two before deciding.

uncertainties: Whether the Kosugi (and Migita) precedent is a priority claim that could require a third laureate or reshape the citation.
Whether the committee would treat Pd C-N coupling as distinct enough from the 2010 cross-coupling prize.
Whether the expert reports on protein electron transfer (B043) would show priority is shared with other protein-ET groups, and whether Winkler should be omitted if only one name could be used.
statement.conflict_note: No formal recusal is apparent from my profile for the preferred configuration (B035). I note a scientific closeness to B043 (protein electron transfer) and B058 (nitrogenase), which sit close to my own work on biological energy conversion, and that Xiaodong Zou is a Stockholm University colleague, although her first-ranked B002 is outside my field. These are disclosed for transparency rather than as grounds for recusal.
